pr_title: cmp.c: Avoid dereference with negative index and use memcpy
pr_body:
This prevents a compile-time warning on newer gcc.

Also fix the warning to print the correct truncated section name.

Fixes #16814
pr_comments: I think an easier fix is to use memcpy() instead.
I have no idea why the change would actually remove the warning, and it seems that if that fixes it, it will come back.

> I have no idea why the change would actually remove the warning, and it seems that if that fixes it, it will come back.

My theory was that the negatively indexed dereferences confuse the compiler to think that they cannot produce valid values.

> I have no idea why the change would actually remove the warning, and it seems that if that fixes it, it will come back.

I agree.  The relevant undefined behavior here comes from accesses and computing pointers outside the boundary of an **object**, but here we know that the containing object extends before the pointer being used for the array dereference (and array dereference is **defined** to be equivalent to pointer addition with dereference).  So it looks like this change is still going to produce the same pointer values and, if there is a real issue with seeking too far in the old code, the new code will have the same behavior.

Agreed this PR is not the answer. The warning itself is talking about truncation. GCC is trying to figure out when the source isn't guaranteed to ​fit in the destination, on grounds that string truncation is probably a bug.
https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2018/05/24/detecting-string-truncation-with-gcc-8

Although their description of what's going on with `strncpy` suggests the code here *should* work. Perhaps "GCC 8 doesn't detect the missing handling in this case but future versions might" has come to pass.
https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2018/05/24/detecting-string-truncation-with-gcc-8#:~:text=Using%20strncpy%20Safely

Regardless, `strncpy` is barely pulling its weight, due to all the weirdnesses around whether the output is or isn't NUL-terminated. `OPENSSL_strlcpy` is less weird, but even that isn't quite right given the source string isn't NUL-terminated to begin with. So it seems this may as well just use `memcpy` at this point.

However, GCC is also right that this is getting truncated! Perhaps an even better solution would be to fix this code to not silently truncate.

> However, GCC is also right that this is getting truncated! Perhaps an even better solution would be to fix this code to not silently truncate.

There is no silent truncation. There is actually a warning (slightly incorrect in the original code) about the possible truncation.
This pull request is ready to merge
Merged to master and 3.0 branches. Thank you for the reviews.

issue_context.title: apps/cmp.c:2009:5: error: 'strncpy' destination unchanged after copying no bytes [-Werror=stringop-truncation]
issue_context.body:
gcc 10.3 to generates this for me:
```
apps/cmp.c: In function 'prev_item.part.0':
apps/cmp.c:2009:5: error: 'strncpy' destination unchanged after copying no bytes [-Werror=stringop-truncation]
 2009 |     strncpy(opt_item, beg, len);
      |     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

The workaround we have for gcc 8 no longer seems to work.

review_comments:
The linked bug points to only the strncpy line , so replacing with memcpy is fine (the beg[-1] did not seem to be a problem).
I don't see much difference between approaches in the while loops though. If anything the new way is probably slightly worse since it points before the start of the buffer before incrementing it back in range.. I think it should be reverted..
Please look again. This is IMO the cleanest way it can be done. And it avoids decrementing the pointer before the start of the buffer.
If I remember correctly, decrementing before the start is undefined.
